title: El rojo es tu color  (Red Is Your Colour)

segments.t: Paquita and Magüi are dressing up for the country wedding of Paquita's ex-husband Paco. Magüi feels shy in her borrowed red cocktail dress, so Paquita cheers her up and suggests taking a photo make Magüi's ex jealous. Listen to the Spanish first.
Venga, Magüi, que no eres la novia.
Seguro que estás guapísima. Sal.
Ya voy.
¿Qué pasa? A ver, mírame.
¡Si estás espectacular! Estás preciosa.
A ver un giro.
El rojo es tu color.
Queda un poco grande.
Vamos a sacarnos una foto para tu ex.
Se la mando. Ven.
Paquita, de verdad, no.
Es que está con Silvia. Silvia es yudoca.
Nos vamos a la boda del ex de Paquita.
A un pueblo, a la boda de Paco.
Let's hear how Paquita encourages Magüi.
Venga, Magüi, que no eres la novia.

'Come on, Magüi, you're not the bride.' The same feminine word means both girlfriend and bride, and context makes it bride here because she is taking ages to get dressed. Notice the casual you form for are.
Seguro que estás guapísima. Sal.
'I'm sure you look gorgeous. Come out.' Adding the extra-strong ending onto pretty turns it into absolutely gorgeous. At the end, a crisp one-syllable command tells Magüi to step out.
Ya voy.

'I'm coming.' Literally already I go: where English says I'm coming from another room, Spanish looks toward the destination and uses I go. It is the standard two-word reply when someone calls your name.
¿Qué pasa? A ver, mírame.

'What's wrong? Let's see, look at me.' Literally what happens, then a tiny two-word chunk meaning let's see, built from to plus see. Look and me join into one word with a written stress mark on the first syllable.
¡Si estás espectacular! Estás preciosa.

'Why, you look spectacular! You look lovely.' Starting an exclamation with the word for if adds warm protest, like saying why, you look amazing when someone doubts herself. Spanish chooses the temporary be form for how someone looks in an outfit.
A ver un giro.
'Let's see a twirl.' After that handy phrase for let's see, the masculine word at the end means a turn or spin. You will also hear this same word in road directions for making a turn.
El rojo es tu color.

'Red is your colour.' When a colour is the subject of a sentence in Spanish, it wears the masculine word for the: literally the red is your colour. Colour itself is spelled identically to British English without the u.
Queda un poco grande.
'It's a little big.' When talking about how clothes fit, Spanish uses a word that elsewhere means stays or remains. With a size word after it, it means fits a little big.
Vamos a sacarnos una foto para tu ex.

'We're going to take a photo for your ex.' In Spain, people usually take a photo using an action word that literally means pull out, tacking on us onto the end because the two of them will be in the picture together.
Se la mando. Ven.

'I'll send it to him. Come here.' Two tiny object words sit side by side before I send: the first stands in for to him, and the feminine second one points to the photo. The final one-syllable command means come.
Paquita, de verdad, no.

'Paquita, really, don't.' Literally of truth, a two-word phrase Spaniards drop into conversation constantly for really, honestly, or I mean it. Putting no at the end pleads with Paquita not to send the picture.
Es que está con Silvia. Silvia es yudoca.

'He's with Silvia. Silvia does judo.' With a person's name after is with, Spanish uses the state form to mean he is dating Silvia. The single word at the end names a judo practitioner of either gender.
Nos vamos a la boda del ex de Paquita.

'We're heading to Paquita's ex's wedding.' Adding the little word for ourselves in front of we go shifts the meaning from simply going to setting off or heading out. Notice how of plus the contracts into one word before ex.
A un pueblo, a la boda de Paco.

'To a village, to Paco's wedding.' The word for village or small country town also means a nation's people in other contexts. Repeating to at the start of both halves builds up where they are bound. Now let's listen to the whole scene again.
Venga, Magüi, que no eres la novia.
Seguro que estás guapísima. Sal.
Ya voy.
¿Qué pasa? A ver, mírame.
¡Si estás espectacular! Estás preciosa.
A ver un giro.
El rojo es tu color.
Queda un poco grande.
Vamos a sacarnos una foto para tu ex.
Se la mando. Ven.
Paquita, de verdad, no.
Es que está con Silvia. Silvia es yudoca.
Nos vamos a la boda del ex de Paquita.
A un pueblo, a la boda de Paco.
You heard how Spanish uses estar when praising how someone looks today, and how colours take 'the' when they lead a sentence. See you in the next scene.
¡Hasta luego!
